articles.title: A job that changed me: I ran observatory tours as a student. An eight-year-old’s question taught me two important lessons
articles.summary: I thought the explanation I’d given about black holes was family-friendly. But, after what she had said, I had to rethink my examples. In the first year of my science degree, I was fortunate to land a job as an astronomy guide at the Sydney Observatory.
body: My favourite object to show in the planetarium was the Hubble Ultra Deep Field image. Before revealing the image, I’d explain how the Hubble space telescope had stared at a piece of sky the size of a grain of sand held at arm’s length for 11 days, collecting enough light to look into the farthest corners of the universe. Then I’d zoom in on that tiny piece of sky, revealing the gorgeous image. At least one person would audibly gasp at the reveal.

But I wasn’t done. I’d get them to spot the spiky objects in the image. There were four obvious stars that were part of our galaxy, the Milky Way. I’d seal the existential crisis by saying: “Those spiky objects are stars. Everything else you see in this image, every blob, every smudge, every tiny speck … is a galaxy.”

On one tour, the clouds were not working with us. So, after showing the group the “stars” through the telescope – the stars on the Australian flag hoisted atop the Sydney Harbour Bridge – I led us down to the 3D theatre. Eventually, the imagination and curiosity of the group took us to the topic of black holes.
points: I thought the explanation I’d given about black holes was family-friendly.

articles.title: The pet I’ll never forget: the tiny horse with a big personality – who helps psychiatric patients
articles.summary: Black Pearl is a therapy animal, who works with military veterans. This sweet show-off has completely changed my life. I trained and competed in dressage for many years and after I retired, I decided to buy a miniature horse for company at home in southern California.
body: I started training her for fun and began to teach her tricks. She learned quickly. I thought of a great way to give back to the community – Black Pearl and I could find ways to help people. I started to wonder where I could visit with my little horse.

Black Pearl inspired me to start my charity, Mini Therapy Horses. If it wasn’t for her outgoing personality, I wouldn’t have attempted it. Now I run a programme with her and eight other miniature therapy horses, visiting patients in the lockdown psychiatric unit at a veterans’ hospital in Los Angeles. The vets have been through so much: they have PTSD, traumatic brain injuries and/or drug addiction and many are homeless. They can pet and hug the horses – they love them. It helps them to feel less lonely and isolated.

We also visit several other hospitals – many of the kids and adults are away from home for a long time and the time they spend with our minis is very comforting. If a child is visually impaired we can take their hands and help them to feel our little horses. They can brush their coats and this tactile experience makes them very happy.
points: Black Pearl is a therapy animal, who works with military veterans.

articles.title: Beyond the Iconic Potato Dish at New NYC Restaurant Somssi
articles.summary: You’ve probably heard of the Potato Potato Potato dish at Somssi, the newest restaurant from Na:eun Hospitality. The triple-layered potato dish is the most labor-intensive dish on the menu but has also become the most popular order, with the kitchen going through up to 100 pounds of potatoes each…
body: Yukon gold potatoes are put through a ricer to become a cream and butter-heavy puree that is set in molds in the freezer. After being toasted in breadcrumbs, the logs of potato are wrapped in russet potato ribbons before being fried up to order.

Next is the ox tongue, which is brined for just over 16 hours before being slow-cooked in herbs, aromatics, and beef tallow for four hours. Huge cuts of tongue are carefully scored so they will get a great sear when they hit the grill. It’s served on a romesco sauce with just a bit of wasabi on the side.

Finally, pork loin is coated in ground shrimp for a creative schnitzel that is reminiscent of shrimp toast. The schnitzel is topped with a sweet-and-sour plum sauce that balances out the thick, crispy fried exterior. Scallop crudo is made up of pressed scallops surrounded with a strawberry sauce and topped off with gooseberries and peppers.
Watch the team at Somssi create creative dishes like a triple-potato bite and a show-stopping grilled tongue dish in this episode of Mise En Place.
points: You’ve probably heard of the Potato Potato Potato dish at Somssi, the newest restaurant from Na:eun Hospitality.

articles.title: Is it true that … drinking alcohol warms you up?
articles.summary: A hot toddy might make you feel toasty, but drinking in cold conditions can be risky. Hot toddies, red wine, a dram of whisky: alcohol has long been a go-to remedy for keeping warm. But while a drink might make you feel warmer, does it actually help?
body: Alcohol affects the body’s temperature-regulating system. Our core body temperature is controlled by the hypothalamus, a region of the brain that helps regulate how we respond to changes in temperature. When we get too hot, blood vessels near the surface of the skin widen, a process known as vasodilation. This allows more warm blood to flow close to the skin, where heat can escape into the surrounding air. When we get too cold, the opposite happens. The blood vessels narrow, or constrict, reducing blood flow to the skin and helping to conserve heat.

Alcohol interferes with this process. It causes blood vessels near the skin to widen, even when our core body temperature has not risen. More warm blood reaches the skin’s surface, which can make us feel hot, and even leave us reaching to take off clothing.
“You’re sending more blood to your skin, which gives you the sensation of feeling warmer,” says Morgan. “But actually you’re not. Your body’s just moving around the blood.”
points: A hot toddy might make you feel toasty, but drinking in cold conditions can be risky.

articles.title: Georgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for sun-dried assassin’s spaghetti | Quick and easy
articles.summary: A spicy, tomatoey pasta that’s cooked like a risotto, but much, much quicker. Popular in Puglia, assassin’s spaghetti is a rich and punchy dish that I just can’t get enough of.
body: Dilute the tomato puree in a litre of just-boiled water and set aside. Put a large frying pan or saute pan that’s wide enough to hold the spaghetti flat on a medium-low heat. Add the oil, garlic and chillies, and fry for a minute, until lightly fragrant. Stir in the sun-dried tomatoes, cook for a couple of minutes, then add the passata and season generously. Simmer vigorously for five minutes, then, once the sauce looks glossy and rich, lay in the spaghetti, spreading it out to cover the bottom of the pan.

Cook on a medium-high heat until the pasta has absorbed the sauce, then ladle in some of the hot tomato broth. Keep cooking until all the liquid has been absorbed, then ladle in more broth. If need be, turn up the heat to high to get a crust underneath and help the pasta absorb the broth. After eight to 10 minutes, use a spatula to flip over the pasta – it should have a slightly charred crust underneath. Keep ladling in more broth, letting it absorb each time before adding more, just like risotto. The pasta should be ready after a further eight to 10 minutes.
points: A spicy, tomatoey pasta that’s cooked like a risotto, but much, much quicker.

articles.title: NYC’s Hottest New Wine Bar Started With a DM Slide
articles.summary: This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants.
body: Giovanni Cervantes and Tania Apolinar spent the last five years slinging tacos at breakneck pace to keep up with the lines at Taqueria Ramírez and Carnitas Ram í rez and rowdy World Cup crowds at Socceria. Now the duo is slowing things down a bit for their first full-service restaurant El Camarón Peludo, a playful wine and seafood spot in the West Village where guests linger over mariscos.
Pre Shift: Where did the idea for El Camarón Peludo come from?

Tania Apolinar: When we were looking at [the space], we considered making it a taqueria, but because of the [long shape of the restaurant], it wouldn’t have worked for that concept. We knew we wanted to do something different, focused on seafood and wine.

Giovanni Cervantes: I was in conversation with Carlos about this idea to serve mariscos in New York when we saw the space. We didn’t know [at the time], but we were setting up the basis of the menu because we were talking about what we like and what we miss a lot [from Mexico]. We also talked about [our past trips] to Europe. We were really interested in how to match [the style of European tapas and wine bars] with what we do, which is the Mexican approach.
points: Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants.

articles.title: Designer Susan Alexandra Made Her Dream Butter Yellow Gown for Her Wedding at a Historic French Villa
articles.summary: Featuring a butter Chihuahua, a communal pavlova, and colorful beaded place settings, the accessories designer’s wedding to Andy Nahman in Biarritz was full of crafty details.
body: Susan Alexandra Korn and Andy Nahman officially met in March 2023, at the writer Naomi Fry’s birthday party in Brooklyn. But as it happens, Susan actually caught Andy’s eye over a year earlier, when he attended the October 2021 opening of the Lower East Side store of her namesake jewelry and accessories brand.

“I walked into this magical polychromatic dream world, well over capacity, with her family, friends, colleagues, and collaborators,” says Andy, who was invited to the opening party by his sister, the writer and editor Haley Nahman. “Susan’s energy was palpable, not only because it was like standing inside her mind’s eye, but in the community surrounding her. I remember going home feeling in awe of her magnetic energy and vision.” But it was at that birthday party, held at the artist Al Freeman’s home, where they really “clicked,” says Susan.
points: Featuring a butter Chihuahua, a communal pavlova, and colorful beaded place settings, the accessories designer’s wedding to Andy Nahman in Biarritz was full of crafty details.

articles.title: Want to Take Your Voting Plan from Drab to Fab? Tack On A Little Treat
articles.summary: Voting in U.S. elections is both an increasingly urgent civic duty and—let’s be honest—a bit of a drag at times. How to combat that? By turning a trip to your polling place into a full-on outing.
body: I’ll be the first to say that voting in American elections is both an increasingly urgent civic duty and, let’s face it, a bit of a drag sometimes. Still, I haven’t missed my chance to vote since I turned 18 (no small feat for a chronic procrastinator with ADHD). My secret? Tacking on something more fun—an embarrassingly over-sweetened seasonal latte at my college coffee shop in Ohio, a mani-pedi at my favorite queer salon in Austin, a shopping trip at Wasteland in Los Angeles—to help get me out the door.

My plan for this year’s midterms has been set in stone for weeks. First, I’ll cast my ballot at the Los Angeles LGBT Center—a wonderful community resource for harm-reduction supplies like Narcan and test strips, as well as theater and breakfast burritos. Then I’ll take the bus to LACMA to check out the new David Geffen Galleries and repair to my favorite Ethiopian spot afterward for injera and a glass of tej.

Would I vote in the midterms even if I couldn’t do anything cute after? Of course. But given the overall grimness of the current political climate, I’m snatching pockets of joy where I can—especially if they’re accessible by public transit.
points: Voting in U.S. elections is both an increasingly urgent civic duty and—let’s be honest—a bit of a drag at times.
By turning a trip to your polling place into a full-on outing.

articles.title: Burgundy Ballet Flats Are Trending—5 Ways to Style Them for Fall
articles.summary: Burgundy ballet flats hit a fall sweet spot: The color is not quite a neutral, but it’s nowhere near as outfit dominating as a punchy shade of red or cobalt.
body: Burgundy has been flexing its might on the fashion scene for quite a few seasons now. We’ve seen the shade crop up on leather jackets and dominate the handbag conversation. Lately, it’s making its way south to ballet flats. Seen at Phoebe Philo, The Row, and Alaïa, burgundy footwear hits a useful sweet spot: It’s not quite a neutral, but it’s nowhere near as outfit dominating as a punchier shade like red or cobalt.

The color feels especially well suited to the ballet flat, a shoe that has become a bona fide wardrobe staple. After seasons of black mesh, metallics, and classic leather styles, burgundy offers a way to make the familiar silhouette feel fresh. It’s also an easy way to introduce a little color into your fall wardrobe. Burgundy flats look just as good with denim, black, brown, and gray as they do with some of the season’s less expected shades, like pale pink or chartreuse.
Below, shop some of our favorites and take a look at the five ways we’re wearing them now.
The Row’s Stella slipper in burgundy lends a fashion-forward finish to classic blue jeans and an everyday wool jacket.
